sec.concepts: The ideas you need to read this network
cat.poll.label: Data request
cat.poll.learn: A sleeping end device wakes up and asks its parent whether a message is waiting for it. This is what reveals who is whose parent.
cat.ack.label: Acknowledgement
cat.ack.learn: Immediate "got it" from the direct neighbour, for one radio hop. Without it the sender tries again. Hidden by default because it is very chatty.
cat.link_status.label: Link status
cat.link_status.learn: Every router tells its direct neighbours (radius 1) how well it hears each of them, every 15 seconds. The network uses it to pick the best paths.
cat.route_request.label: Route request
cat.route_request.learn: A network command flooded through all routers. From the coordinator it is probably a "many-to-one" announcement: it tells the whole network how to reach it.
cat.route_record.label: Route record (probable)
cat.route_record.learn: A command sent to the coordinator. Each relay appends its own address, so the frame grows by 2 bytes per hop. The coordinator learns the way back.
cat.data_direct.label: Direct data
cat.data_direct.learn: An application message (measurement, command) delivered in a single hop: the radio sender is the author and the radio receiver is the recipient.
cat.data_multihop.label: Relayed data
cat.data_multihop.learn: An application message on a multi-hop path: the radio address (MAC) differs from the author or the final recipient (NWK). A router is in the middle.
cat.broadcast.label: Broadcast
cat.broadcast.learn: A message for everyone. Each router repeats it once, which carries it across the whole network. Any router does this.
cat.beacon_req.label: Network search
cat.beacon_req.learn: A device looking for a network to join, or to find again, asks nearby routers to show themselves.
cat.beacon.label: Beacon
cat.beacon.learn: A router's answer to a network search. It says in clear whether it still accepts routers and end devices as children, and whether joining is open.
cat.join.label: Association
cat.join.learn: A device asks a router to become its parent, and the router answers. The outcome (accepted, network full, denied) travels in clear.
cat.nwk_cmd.label: Network command
cat.nwk_cmd.learn: Another network-layer command (leave, rejoin, route error…). Without the network key its exact type is encrypted; with it, the log names the command and what it says.
cat.mac_cmd.label: Radio command
cat.no_data.label: Nothing waiting
cat.no_data.learn: An empty frame from a parent to the end device that just polled it: its acknowledgement said a message might be waiting, and there was none after all. Legitimate (IEEE 802.15.4). Hidden by default because it follows polls.
cat.inter_pan.label: Inter-PAN
cat.inter_pan.learn: A frame sent outside any network, between devices that do not share a PAN yet: Touchlink commissioning (a remote paired right next to a bulb), for instance. Its network header is reduced to its frame control.
cat.green_power.label: Green Power
cat.green_power.learn: A frame from a battery-free Green Power device (a kinetic switch, for instance), relayed into the network by a Green Power proxy. Its source id travels in clear.
cat.foreign.label: Neighbouring network
cat.foreign.learn: A frame from another 802.15.4 network on the same channel (different PAN id), a neighbour's for instance. It is not part of your network and is kept off the map.
cat.other.label: Not decoded
cat.other.learn: An 802.15.4 frame that is not readable Zigbee: another protocol, MAC-layer security, or a damaged frame. This is normal and nothing to worry about.
explain.poll: {src} wakes up and asks its parent {dst} whether a message is waiting.
explain.ack: {src} confirms to {dst} that the previous frame arrived.
explain.ack.pending: {src} confirms to {dst} that the request arrived, and says a message is waiting for it.
explain.link_status: {src} tells its direct neighbours how well it hears them.
explain.route_request.relay: {src} repeats the route request from {author} (radius left {radius}).
explain.route_request.origin: {author} floods a route request to the whole network (radius {radius}).
explain.route_record.relay: {src} relays to {dst} the route record of {author}, adding its own address ({bytes} bytes).
explain.route_record.origin: {author} sends its path to the coordinator through {dst} ({bytes} bytes).
explain.data_direct: {author} sends an encrypted message straight to {target}.
explain.data_multihop.relay: {src} relays a message from {author} meant for {target}, handing it to {dst}.
explain.broadcast.relay: {src} repeats a broadcast from {author} to spread it.
explain.beacon_req: A device is looking for a network and asks nearby routers to show themselves.
explain.beacon: {src} shows itself. Accepts routers: {zr}. Accepts end devices: {zed}. Joining open: {permit}.
explain.nwk_cmd: {author} sends a network command to {target}. Its type is encrypted.
explain.foreign: Frame from a neighbouring network (PAN {pan}). It does not concern your network.
explain.retry: Sent again: the first attempt was not acknowledged.
nwkx.route_request: It looks for a path to {dst}.
nwkx.route_reply: It carries back a path from {originator} to {responder}; cost accumulated so far: {cost} (each link counts from 1, excellent, to 7, very poor).
nwkx.leave.request: It asks the recipient to leave the network.
nwkx.leave.rejoin: It leaves and will rejoin right away.
nwkx.ed_timeout_request: It asks its parent to keep it as a child for {time} without news.
nwkstatus.5: no room to hold messages for sleeping children
nwkstatus.6: a message for a sleeping child expired
anim.1.title: A dot running along a line
anim.1.body: A frame addressed to one device: the dot leaves the radio sender and reaches the radio receiver. When a message crosses several routers you see the dots chain up, one hop after the other.
anim.2.title: A widening ring
anim.2.body: A broadcast: the device talks to everyone in range. The small regular teal rings are each router's link status. A large ring repeated from node to node is a broadcast spreading.
anim.3.title: A dotted line
anim.3.body: The parent-child relation, deduced from data requests: a battery device always polls its parent.
anim.4.title: A solid line
anim.4.body: A radio hop that addressed traffic has already used. It lights up on every passage, then fades.
anim.5.title: A line with a percentage, and nodes pushed apart
anim.5.body: A link on which frames often have to be sent again. The percentage is the share of retransmissions, and the map stretches that link: devices that hear each other badly drift apart.
concepts.1.title: Three roles
concepts.1.body: The **coordinator** creates the network and runs it. **Routers** are mains-powered (plugs, meters) and forward other devices' messages. **End devices** (sensors, radiator valves) sleep to save their battery and go through a "parent" router.
concepts.2.title: Two layers of addresses
concepts.2.body: Every frame carries two pairs of addresses. The **MAC** layer says who transmits and who receives *this radio hop*. The **NWK** layer says who wrote the message and who it is finally for. When they differ, a router is relaying.
concepts.3.title: Short address and IEEE
concepts.3.body: The **short** address (like 0x2B01) is handed out when a device joins and can change. The **IEEE** address (64 bits) is burnt into the chip. It travels in the security header of each hop, which is how a short address is tied to a name, and its first bytes tell who made the radio chip.
concepts.4.title: Radius
concepts.4.body: The **radius** is the number of hops left. Every relaying router decreases it by 1. A broadcast that starts at 10 and shows up again at 9, then 8, is spreading through the mesh.
concepts.5.title: Encryption
concepts.5.body: Everything after the NWK header is encrypted with the network key, and this tool leaves it that way. You see who talks to whom, when and how much, never the content. Network commands are recognised by their shape, and marked "probable" when that is a deduction.
concepts.6.title: Link quality, seen from outside
concepts.6.body: Each router measures how well it hears its neighbours, but it shares those figures in encrypted frames. What can be seen from outside is the result: a frame sent **again** means its acknowledgement never came back. Many retransmissions on a link mean a poor link.
concepts.7.title: Is a router overloaded?
concepts.7.body: A router's memory cannot be read from the air. Its symptoms can: the time between receiving a frame and relaying it, frames it never relays, and messages it holds for a sleeping child that are never collected.
concepts.8.title: What the sniffer hears
concepts.8.body: The dongle only hears what reaches it. A distant device may be missing from the map, and the power shown (dBm) is what the sniffer received, not the link quality between two devices.

sec.title: Security
sec.test.title: Is your network using the default key?
sec.test.help: Many Zigbee networks hand out their network key during a join, wrapped in a link key that is the same public value on every device. Anyone in radio range who catches a join can then read everything. This test watches joins and tells you which case you are in. It only listens; it changes nothing.
sec.step.1: Leave this page running on the right channel.
sec.step.2: Make one device **re-join**: remove it from your hub and pair it again, or reset the device. A join has to happen on the air for the test to see anything.
sec.step.3: Read the verdict above. A device that never re-joins cannot be tested.
sec.verdict.untested: No join seen yet — nothing to judge.
sec.verdict.vulnBody: A join was secured with the **default** link key, so the network key below was recovered straight from the air. Anyone nearby can do the same. Re-pair your devices with an install code if your hub supports it.
sec.verdict.safeBody: A join was seen, and it was secured with a key that is *not* the public default. The network key could not be recovered from it.
sec.verdict.touchlinkBody: A Touchlink (ZLL) commissioning exchange carried this network's key, encrypted with the publicly known ZLL master key, so it was recovered straight from the air. Anyone nearby who triggers or overhears a Touchlink join can do the same. Pairing through your hub's normal (Trust-Center) join instead of Touchlink avoids this.
sec.key.title: Network key
sec.key.help: With the network key, this tool decrypts your own traffic to show each device's reported model and the link costs the routers measure. The key stays in memory on this computer: it is never saved or sent.
sec.key.label: Network key (32 hex characters)
sec.key.none: No key: the map shows only what is readable without one.
sec.key.recovered: Key recovered from your network's own traffic.
sec.save.title: Save this key
sec.save.help: Keep the recovered network key so every later session on this network decrypts automatically. Stored on this computer only.
sec.save.done: Saved for {pan}. It will be used automatically next time.

hue.title: Hue Bridge
hue.help: Optional. Once your bridge is set up, the tool reads from it each device's name, model, type, room, battery and whether the bridge can reach it, and shows them next to what the sniffer hears. Nothing is contacted until you act here. The application key stays in a private file on this computer and is never shown. The bridge reports no link quality, so none is shown.
hue.trust: The bridge's certificate is recorded the first time you set it up and must be the same ever after. A different one is refused until you forget the bridge.
hue.status.ok: Bridge “{name}” ({id}) is set up. Last read at {time}.
hue.status.never: Bridge “{name}” ({id}) is set up. Not read yet.
hue.status.channel: Its network is on Zigbee channel {channel}.
hue.waiting: Press the link button on the bridge now. Waiting for it, up to 30 seconds…
hue.timeout: The link button was not pressed in time. Click Pair again, then press the button.
hue.finding: Searching the network for a few seconds…
hue.found.none: No bridge answered. The search often cannot cross into a container or a virtual machine: type the address instead.
hue.host: Bridge address (IP address, name, or address:port)
hue.pair.help: Click Pair, then press the big button on the bridge. The tool asks the bridge for a key every two seconds, for up to 30 seconds.
hue.key: Or enter an application key you already have

hue.s.unknown: in a state this tool does not know

login.title: Sign in
login.intro: This map shows the radio traffic of your network. Enter the password this server was started with.
login.error: That password was not accepted. If you have tried several times, wait a minute before trying again.
login.signout.help: Ends this browser's session on the server. The next visit asks for the password again.
